rename.from: Unable to sort on user enforced index
rename.to: [YCQL] Unable to do explicit ORDER BY sort on clustered columns of index

body:
Thx @dwheeler for reporting.
@nocaway - could you take an initial look of what's involved to address this?

This is a bug in YugaByte semantic analysis.
- The error check was processing SELECT statement against the table description without considering the secondary indexes of the table.
- The decision on which index to use for a query is determined at a later time.

Implementation.
- Currently, when WHERE clause is processed, values of columns are divided to list<hash_column>, list<range_column>, and list<regular_column> according to the table description.  These lists are then used to check against ONLY the PRIMARY index. Afterward, YugaByte walks the lists to decide which INDEX to use, but by that time, the error check already rejects the requested query.

- The fix would be changing the list<column> to array< list<column> >.  Each entry of the array would be associated with an index.  PRIMARY index is associated with array[0].  Index id 1 would be associated with array[1], and so on. The array can then be used to analyze the query against each INDEX.

This has been fixed by commit https://github.com/YugaByte/yugabyte-db/commit/592fcfab8a8bd6a78fbf6438f307ed9af3b5b97f

Instead of making copies of column_list (schema) for the indexes as suggested in my previous comment, the existing code made one new copy for the entire SELECT statement, replace the target-table with its chosen table_index, and rerun analysis on the entire SELECT against the chosen table_index.  I decided to keep this design of copying the entire SELECT statement in this bug fix as changing the current design would be beyond the scope of this bug fix.

To fix the issue, the analysis for ORDER BY clause is now done after the aforementioned copy of original SELECT statement is created and being analyzed.  As a result, the error-check is run against the index schema instead of the schema of the target-table.

issue.body:
Jira Link: [DB-2204](https://yugabyte.atlassian.net/browse/DB-2204)
Typical trying to create table and index:

```cql
CREATE TABLE t (i int PRIMARY KEY, j int);
CREATE INDEX ON t (j);
```

```
InvalidRequest: Error from server: code=2200 [Invalid query] message="Invalid Table Definition. Transactions cannot be enabled in an index of a table without transactions enabled.
CREATE INDEX ON t (j);
^^^^^^
 (ql error -302)"
```

Okay...  Look at [the documentation][1] and find

> `WITH transactions = { 'enabled' : true };`

Let's try it with false to disable transactions.

```cql
CREATE INDEX ON t (j) WITH transactions = { 'enabled' : false };
```

```
ycqlsh:k> CREATE INDEX ON t (j) WITH transactions = { 'enabled' : false };
InvalidRequest: Error from server: code=2200 [Invalid query] message="Invalid Table Definition. Consistency level must be user-enforced in an index without transactions enabled.
CREATE INDEX ON t (j) WITH transactions = { 'enabled' : false };
^^^^^^
 (ql error -302)"
```

Okay...  Look at [the documentation][1] again, but don't find anything about "consistency level" or "user enforced" (search terms "consistency" and "enforced" don't show up on the page at all).

Go to GitHub issues and search until coming up with [a good query][2] leading to issue #1591 that shows

> `transactions = {'enabled' : FALSE, 'consistency_level' : 'user_enforced'};`

Let's try it with that.

```cql
CREATE INDEX ON t (j) WITH transactions = { 'enabled' : false, 'consistency_level' : 'user_enforced' };
DESC t;
```

```
CREATE TABLE k.t (
    i int PRIMARY KEY,
    j int
) WITH default_time_to_live = 0
    AND transactions = {'enabled': 'false'};
CREATE INDEX t_j_idx ON k.t (j, i)
    WITH transactions = {'enabled': 'false', 'consistency_level': 'user_enforced'};
```

Finally works.  If one has no idea and doesn't care what transactions and user enforced are, the steps one has to take to make it work are not fun.  This information should be clear in the docs (even `WITH transactions` isn't in the grammar at the top of the page).

[1]: https://docs.yugabyte.com/latest/api/ycql/ddl_create_index/
[2]: https://github.com/yugabyte/yugabyte-db/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+Consistency+level+must+be+user-enforced+in+an+index+without+

issue.body:
Used for higher performance of writes in inserts where consistency semantics can be relaxed. Typically used in streaming apps where high ingest is required.

## Details

**Main caveat: If an insert/update or batch of such operations fails, it is the app's responsibility to retry the operation so that the index is consistent.** Much like in a 2-table case, it would have been the apps responsibility to retry (in case of a failure between the update to the two tables) to make sure both tables are in sync again.

Main advantage of this approach rather than you having to use a second table is for UPDATE cases where the old index record has to be deleted from the table, and so would be an extra roundtrip to the database.

## Example

Notice that here the table is not marked with transactions enabled. And the index has the 'consistency_level' : 'user_enforced'  clause. # Example

```
create table example (
  ...,
  PRIMARY KEY (...)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (...)
   AND transactions = { 'enabled' : false };

CREATE INDEX example_index ON example (...) INCLUDE (cluster_size)
    WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY(...)
    AND transactions = { 'enabled' : false, 'consistency_level' : 'user_enforced' };
```
